comment: The ten markets. Eight shares, Franklin Templeton's BENJI and gold.
Each one is a stand-in token this repository mints until DTCC's land; the
prices are real.
EVERY MARKET CARRIES THE SAME 7000 bps OF LTV, and that is the design, not a
shortcut. On a normal lending market the LTV is a bet on how far the
collateral can fall before anyone reacts, so a volatile share gets 30% and a
money fund gets 70%. Here the debt is not left alone to be overtaken by the
price: the borrowed USDC sits in the Agama vault as shares, and the agents
hold the target both ways. The stock rises and they borrow the difference;
it falls and they repay out of the vault shares, never by selling the stock.
Liquidation itself repays out of those shares first and only calls a
liquidator if that was not enough.
So what backs the loan is not the share's calm, it is the position's own
counterweight, and that is the same on Tesla as on a money fund. What is
left of the share's volatility is the part the agents cannot outrun: the gap
when the session is shut. That is what `offHoursBuffer` is for, and it is
the one number that still differs by asset.
A loop at L times carries an LTV of (L - 1) / L, so 7000 bps is a ceiling of
3.33x on every market, Tesla included.
`feed` is the RedStone data service feed id. BENJI is a NAV feed, not a DEX
price: a fund share has no market, it has a net asset value, and RedStone
publishes it as such. Gold is a cross, XAU/USD.

markets.name: Franklin OnChain U.S. Government Money Fund

redstoneNote: The on-chain feed id is the name inside the signed payload, not the ticker. RedStone carries SPY only as SPY---PRE_AFTER, BENJI as BENJI_ETHEREUM_FUNDAMENTAL and gold as XAU. Binding the oracle to the ticker instead is what left two markets admin-priced in the first deployment.
